content: Ina May Gaskin is a Certified Professional Midwife (CPM) who is often referred to as the mother of authentic midwifery. In 1971, she and her husband, Stephen Gaskin, established The Farm, an intentional community located in Summertown, Tennessee. Within this community, she and a group of midwives created one of the first out-of-hospital birth centers in the United States. The birthing practices at The Farm adhere to the guidelines recommended by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. During births at The Farm, family members and friends are typically present and are encouraged to actively participate in the birthing process. Carol Lorente, in 1995, noted that the influence of Gaskin and her team of midwives was significantly amplified by the publication of her book Spiritual Midwifery in 1977. Ina May Gaskin is credited with the rise and popularization of direct-entry midwifery in the United States, beginning in the early 1970s. She is also the publisher of the periodical Birth Gazette and is recognized internationally as a speaker on maternity care issues, often representing the Midwives Alliance of North America (MANA). Gaskin has spoken at events such as the Starwood Festival and the WinterStar Symposium, where she has discussed the history and significance of midwifery. Additionally, she founded the Safe Motherhood Quilt Project, a national initiative aimed at raising awareness about maternal mortality rates and honoring women who have died from pregnancy-related causes over the past two decades. Her book Ina May's Guide to Childbirth was published in 2003. A study conducted by Durand in 1992 examined the outcomes of 1,707 home births attended by midwives at The Farm between 1971 and 1989. These outcomes were compared to those of over 14,000 hospital births attended by physicians in 1980. The study analyzed perinatal mortality rates, labor complications, and the use of assisted delivery methods. It concluded that, under specific conditions, home births attended by lay midwives can be as safe as, and involve fewer interventions than, hospital births attended by physicians. Ina May Gaskin has delivered lectures at midwifery conferences and medical schools worldwide. She served as the President of the Midwives Alliance of North America from 1996 to 2002. Her contributions have been recognized with several awards, including the ASPO/Lamaze Irwin Chabon Award in 1997 and the Tennessee Perinatal Association Recognition Award. In the same year, she was named a Visiting Fellow of Morse College at Yale University. Her published works include: Babies, Breastfeeding & Bonding (1987) Spiritual Midwifery (first edition in 1977, reissued in 2002) Ina May's Guide to Childbirth (2003) She has also authored several articles, including: Induced and Seduced: The Dangers of Cytotec (Mothering, July-August 2001) The Undervalued Art of Vaginal Breech Birth: A Skill Every Birth Attendant Should Learn (Mothering, July-August 2004) A Summary of Articles Published in English about Misoprostol (Cytotec) for Cervical Ripening or Induction of Labor (2005) Ina May Gaskin is widely regarded as an author, activist, and innovator in the field of midwifery.
